name: relaybell
author: relaybell

sections.description:
relaybell adds browser push notifications to any WordPress site. Visitors opt in
with a native prompt, and you reach them again with a click — no app, no email
address required.

Core

  • One-click Connect to relaybell — sign in (or create a free account),
    approve your site, and you’re back in WordPress, connected. Nothing to copy.
  • A status panel that checks everything for you: connection, HTTPS, your
    relaybell account, the relaybell script, the service worker, whether
    relaybell runs on your public pages and whether a page cache still serves
    visitors an older copy — with a plain-English fix for anything that isn’t
    right.
  • Opt-in prompt powered by the relaybell browser SDK.
  • Automatic push when you publish — choose which post types, attach the featured
    image, and optionally send each post only to subscribers of the relaybell
    topic named like its primary category (create those topics in relaybell
    first; visitors choose topics in the box opened by
    RelayBell.showPreferences()).
  • Clears the page caches of common caching plugins and hosts when you connect,
    disconnect or update, so visitors get the current set-up.
  • The service worker ships as a static file inside the plugin, so it works with
    any permalink setting and web server, and alongside PWA plugins.
  • Identify logged-in users by account email so behavioral and cross-device
    targeting work (filterable to a hashed id).

WooCommerce

When WooCommerce is active, relaybell automatically fires behavioral events to
your relaybell project — no code, just save an API key. Each event can be toggled
on or off under Settings → relaybell:

  • purchase — order paid or completed (de-duplicated per order).
  • cart.updated — item added to cart (logged-in shoppers).
  • back_in_stock — a product or variation is back in stock; relaybell alerts
    everyone on its waitlist.
  • price_drop — a product’s price falls below the last price relaybell saw;
    relaybell alerts shoppers who viewed, carted or wait-listed it.
  • signup — a new customer / user registers.
  • checkout.started — an order is created at checkout (classic checkout or the
    Checkout block), once per order.
  • order.refunded — an order is refunded.

It also adds an optional “Notify me when back in stock” button on
out-of-stock product pages (and for out-of-stock options of variable products)
that subscribes the shopper and puts them on that product’s waitlist.

Events are sent at the very end of the request, after the page has been built
(on PHP-FPM and LiteSpeed servers, after it has been delivered), so your store’s
pages never wait for relaybell.

HPOS (High-Performance Order Storage / custom order tables) is fully supported.

External services

This plugin connects to relaybell (https://relaybell.com), a web push
notification service operated by Nexistech. relaybell is required for the plugin
to function: browser push notifications cannot be stored or delivered without a
push service, and this plugin is the WordPress client for that service. You need
a relaybell account and API key to use the plugin.

1. The relaybell browser SDK (https://relaybell.com/relaybell-sdk.js)

The SDK script is loaded on your site’s front end so visitors can opt in to push
notifications. This happens on page load, for every visitor, once you have saved
a Project ID. On each page view the SDK also fetches your project’s public
settings (GET https://relaybell.com/api/v1/projects/{project id}/config: the push
key and the prompt and on-site message settings you chose in relaybell). The
visitor’s browser sends its normal request data to relaybell (IP address, user
agent and your site’s address) with these requests.

If you set them up in your relaybell dashboard, the SDK also reports, without any
personal data: which version of an A/B-tested opt-in prompt was shown (POST
…/prompt-event), and views and clicks of on-site messages (POST
…/onsite-event: the message id and whether it was viewed or clicked).

2. Subscribing a visitor (POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/projects/{project id}/subscriptions)

When a visitor accepts the browser’s notification prompt, the SDK sends their
push subscription to relaybell: the browser-issued push endpoint URL and its
encryption keys, plus the page URL, the browser’s language and time zone, which
prompt version they saw, and any topic or tags you have configured. For
logged-in users the plugin also sends their WordPress role as a tag. If the
browser later replaces a subscription on its own, the service worker re-sends it
(with the old endpoint) in the background. If the visitor later changes their topics in the box opened by
RelayBell.showPreferences(), the SDK saves the choice (GET/POST
…/preferences).
If the visitor is logged in to WordPress, their account email is also sent as an
externalId so you can target them across devices — you can replace this with a
hashed value using the relaybell_external_id filter, or remove it entirely
(turn off “Link subscribers to their account email”). This is only sent for
logged-in users (never for site administrators), and only after the visitor has
opted in to notifications. It comes with a userHash, a signature your server
makes from the id (see 9 below), so relaybell can tell the id really comes from
your site.

3. Sending notifications (POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/notifications)

When you publish a post (if “Send on publish” is enabled), the post title, the
first 20 words of its text, its permalink and featured image URL (and, with
“Category → topic” on, the matching relaybell topic) are sent to relaybell so it
can build the notification. Your API key authenticates the request.
Password-protected posts are never sent.

4. WooCommerce events from your server (POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/events)

If WooCommerce is active, your server sends commerce events to relaybell,
authenticated with your API key: an order’s id, total and currency (purchase,
checkout.started, and order.refunded with the refunded amount); the product’s
name, id and page URL plus the cart’s value (cart.updated); a new user’s id
(signup); and a product’s name, id and page URL (back_in_stock), plus its old
and new price (price_drop). Each is sent at the end of the request that
triggered it. These events are enabled by default once WooCommerce is
active and the site is connected; each one can be turned off individually under
Settings → relaybell.

While Link subscribers to their account email is on, the customer’s email —
the account email for a registered customer, otherwise the order’s billing email,
or whatever your relaybell_external_id filter returns instead — is sent with
purchase, checkout.started, cart.updated, signup and order.refunded
events, so relaybell can match them to the shopper’s subscription. With it off,
those events are sent without it and cart.updated is not sent at all.
cart.updated is never sent for shoppers who aren’t logged in; for a guest
order, the billing email is used. back_in_stock and price_drop
describe a product and never include customer data.

5. Shopper interest from product pages (POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/projects/{project id}/events)

On WooCommerce product pages, the visitor’s browser sends two events to relaybell:

  • waitlist.join — when the visitor clicks Notify me when back in stock and
    allows notifications.
  • product.viewed — when a visitor who is already subscribed opens a product page
    (only while the Price drop event is on).

Each sends your relaybell project id, the product id (or the chosen variation’s
id), the browser’s push endpoint URL, and — when “Link subscribers to their
account email” is on and the visitor is logged in — their external id (account
email, or your filtered value). Nothing is sent for visitors who haven’t
subscribed to notifications.

6. Delivery and click reports (POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/notifications/{id}/receipt and /click)

When a notification reaches a subscriber’s browser, and when they click it, the
service worker reports it to relaybell for delivery and click-through stats. The
report contains the notification id, a signed token and the subscription’s id —
no page content or personal data.

7. Connecting your site (https://relaybell.com/connect/wordpress and POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/connect/exchange)

When an administrator clicks Connect to relaybell, their browser is sent to
relaybell with your site’s address, site name, the wp-admin return address and
a one-time security value. After they approve, relaybell returns a one-time code,
and your server exchanges it (sending the code and your site address) for your
relaybell Project ID and an API key, which are saved in your site’s database.

8. Admin status and test push (GET/POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/…)

The status panel on Settings → relaybell checks your connection and shows
your subscriber count (GET /api/v1/stats), checks that your Project ID belongs
to your API key (GET /api/v1/me), and shows when relaybell last ran on your
public pages (GET /api/v1/setup-status) — all from your server, with your API
key. The panel also loads the relaybell script and your project’s public
settings (GET …/projects/{project id}/config) in the administrator’s browser,
to confirm they aren’t blocked (the script is only fetched there, not run), and your server fetches your own home page once
in a while (like a visitor, without cookies) to tell whether a page cache still
serves an older copy; that request stays on your site.

While the “verify your relaybell email” notice is shown, the Plugins screen
re-checks it in the background at most once an hour (GET
/api/v1/stats, and GET /api/v1/me).

Advanced → relaybell host changes where all of the requests in this
section go (for relaybell-provided hosts only). It must be an https:// address.

Subscribe this browser subscribes the administrator’s own browser the same
way a visitor subscribes (see 2), then your server marks that browser as your
test device (POST /api/v1/test-devices: its push endpoint URL). Send test
push asks relaybell to send a test notification to your test devices only
(POST /api/v1/test-devices/send: the test title and text, and your home page
address). These only run in wp-admin, when an administrator uses them.

If you open a “send test to my device” link from your relaybell dashboard on your
site, the SDK registers that browser as one of your test devices (POST
/api/v1/test-devices/claim: the code from the link and the browser’s push
endpoint URL).

9. Verifying visitor sign-in IDs (GET and PUT https://relaybell.com/api/v1/identity)

So nobody can pretend to be one of your customers to get their notifications,
your server fetches your project’s identity secret from relaybell with your API
key — when you connect, when you open Settings → relaybell, and once a day —
and keeps it in your site’s database. The first time, it also asks relaybell to
accept only verified sign-in IDs for your project (you can turn this off in your
relaybell dashboard under Settings → Developer). The secret is used on your
server to sign logged-in visitors’ IDs; it is never put in your pages. No visitor
data is sent with these requests.

10. Disconnecting (DELETE https://relaybell.com/api/v1/keys/current)

When an administrator clicks Disconnect, your server asks relaybell to cancel
the API key that one-click Connect created for this site, so a copy left in a
backup can’t be used. Only the key itself is sent (as the request’s
authorization). A key you entered by hand is left alone.

No data is sent anywhere until you connect (or save a Project ID and API key
manually).

Service provider: Nexistech (https://nexistech.in)
Terms of service: https://relaybell.com/terms
Privacy policy: https://relaybell.com/privacy
Data processing agreement: https://relaybell.com/dpa
sections.installation:
1. Upload the relaybell folder to /wp-content/plugins/, or install the ZIP
    from Plugins → Add New → Upload Plugin.
  2. Activate relaybell.
  3. Go to Settings → relaybell and click Connect to relaybell. Sign in
    (or create a free account), approve your site, and you’ll land back in
    WordPress connected.
  4. Optionally enable Send on publish and pick which post types push.

Your site must use HTTPS — browsers only allow push notifications on secure
sites (and on localhost for testing). The status panel tells you if anything
needs attention.

The WooCommerce bridge auto-loads when WooCommerce is active — there is nothing
extra to set up.
sections.faq:
Do I need WooCommerce?

No. Without WooCommerce you still get the opt-in prompt and publish-time pushes.
The commerce events simply activate when WooCommerce is present.

Do subscribers need to give an email address?

No. Web push works from the browser subscription alone. If a user is logged in,
relaybell also binds their account email as an externalId for richer targeting;
you can substitute a hashed value with the relaybell_external_id filter.

How do I send a test notification?

On Settings → relaybell, click Subscribe this browser (allow notifications
when your browser asks), then Send test push. The test goes only to your own
browser — never to your subscribers — and appears within a few seconds. The
settings page then tells you whether it reached this browser, and what to check
if you don’t see it.

If no permission pop-up appears, look for a bell icon in the address bar and
choose Allow. If notifications are blocked, the status panel explains how to
unblock them.

The test push works, but my visitors never get my posts

Most often your relaybell account email isn’t verified yet. Until it is,
relaybell doesn’t send anything to your visitors — new-post pushes, campaigns
and automations are all held back — while test pushes to your own browser still
work. Click the link in the email relaybell sent when you signed up (check your
spam folder), or send it again from your relaybell dashboard. The status panel
and the Plugins screen show a red warning while this is the case.

Also check that Send on publish is turned on (it is off by default) and,
if you use Category → topic, that relaybell has a topic for the post’s
category. Password-protected posts are never pushed.

I use a page cache or a CDN — do I need to do anything?

relaybell’s set-up is part of every page, so a cached page keeps the set-up it
was saved with. When you connect, disconnect, change the connection or update
the plugin, relaybell clears the cache of WP Rocket, LiteSpeed Cache, W3 Total
Cache, WP Super Cache, SiteGround Speed Optimizer, Breeze, Nginx Helper, Cache
Enabler, WP Fastest Cache, WP-Optimize, Hummingbird, WP Engine and Kinsta. If
your host or a CDN such as Cloudflare caches your pages too, clear that cache
yourself. The status panel warns when visitors still get an older copy, and
shows when relaybell last ran on your public pages. (Developers: other caches
can hook into relaybell_purge_page_caches.)

How does “Category → topic” work?

With it on, each new post is sent only to subscribers who follow the relaybell
topic named like the post’s primary category — for example a topic “Tech News”
for the category tech-news. Create those topics in your relaybell dashboard
(Audience → Topics) first: a post whose category has no matching topic isn’t
pushed. Visitors choose their topics in the box your site opens with
RelayBell.showPreferences() (for example from a “Notification settings” link).

The status panel says my site isn’t on HTTPS

Browsers only allow push notifications on HTTPS sites, plus localhost for
development. Enable HTTPS (most hosts offer a free certificate), and make sure
both addresses under Settings → General start with https://.

Connect doesn’t work on my server

Your server must be able to make outgoing HTTPS requests to relaybell.com. If
your host blocks that, open Advanced on the settings page and enter your
Project ID and an API key from the relaybell dashboard manually.

Does it support HPOS (custom order tables)?

Yes. The plugin declares custom_order_tables compatibility and uses the
WooCommerce CRUD APIs throughout.

Which hooks/filters can I use?

  • relaybell_external_id — swap the account email for a hashed id. Also applied
    to the customer email sent with WooCommerce events ($user is null for a guest
    order).
  • relaybell_sdk_init — modify the full SDK init options. For a logged-in
    visitor the plugin identified, the userHash for the externalId you return is
    added afterwards.
  • relaybell_user_hash( $external_id ) (function) — the userHash for an id your
    own code passes to relaybell (e.g. to RelayBell.identify( id, hash )), so
    relaybell accepts it while User ID verification is on.
  • relaybell_publish_payload — modify the publish push body.
  • relaybell_category_topic — map a post’s primary category to a relaybell
    topic (its slug, or its id).
  • relaybell_woo_event_payload — modify any commerce event body before sending.
  • relaybell_purge_page_caches (action) — clear a page cache or CDN relaybell
    doesn’t know, whenever relaybell clears page caches.
sections.changelog:
1.2.6

  • Change: the “Connect relaybell” and “account email isn’t verified” notices now
    appear only on the Plugins screen, only for administrators, and can be dismissed
    for good. They no longer appear on the Dashboard. Settings → relaybell keeps
    showing the same status.

1.2.5

  • Change: the settings page’s styles and scripts are now regular files
    (assets/relaybell-admin.css, assets/relaybell-admin.js,
    assets/relaybell-notice.js) loaded through WordPress’s script and style
    queues, instead of being printed into the page. The page works exactly as
    before.
  • Change: the “Notify me when back in stock” button’s markup is escaped when it
    is printed.
  • Fix: the status panel now says “1 subscriber” instead of “1 subscribers”.
  • Change: the status panel checks that the relaybell script is reachable without
    running it in wp-admin, and the Disconnect confirmation is part of the
    settings script.
  • Change: the relaybell host (Advanced) must be an https:// address, and the
    home-page cache check keeps TLS certificate checks on.
  • Change: the clean-up that runs when you delete the plugin uses prepared
    database queries. It removes the same data as before.
  • Docs: “External services” now lists every request, including the opt-in
    prompt and on-site message stats, topic preferences, test devices and
    cancelling the API key on disconnect.
  • Docs: older changelog entries moved to changelog.txt.

1.2.4

  • Security: someone could send relaybell a logged-in customer’s email from their
    own browser and then get that customer’s notifications (cart reminders and other
    personal pushes). Your site now signs each logged-in visitor’s ID with a secret
    only your server and relaybell know, and the plugin turns on relaybell’s User ID
    verification for your project, so an ID without a valid signature is ignored.
    It picks up the secret when you connect, when you open Settings → relaybell, and
    once a day. Nothing to set up.
  • New: a status row on Settings → relaybell says whether visitor sign-in IDs are
    verified.
  • New: relaybell_user_hash() for themes and plugins that pass their own IDs to
    relaybell.

1.2.3

  • Fix: password-protected posts no longer send a push when they are published.
    Before, the push showed the start of the protected text to every subscriber.
  • Fix: posts published from the block editor now show their featured image in
    the push. The push now goes out once WordPress has finished saving the post,
    with its image and categories, and still only once per post.
  • Fix: deleting the plugin on a multisite network with more than 100 sites now
    removes relaybell’s settings and API key from every site, not only the first
    100.

Older versions are listed in changelog.txt in the plugin folder.

If you open a “send test to my device” link from your relaybell dashboard on your
site, the SDK registers that browser as one of your test devices (POST
/api/v1/test-devices/claim: the code from the link and the browser’s push
endpoint URL).

9. Verifying visitor sign-in IDs (GET and PUT https://relaybell.com/api/v1/identity)

So nobody can pretend to be one of your customers to get their notifications,
your server fetches your project’s identity secret from relaybell with your API
key — when you connect, when you open Settings → relaybell, and once a day —
and keeps it in your site’s database. The first time, it also asks relaybell to
accept only verified sign-in IDs for your project (you can turn this off in your
relaybell dashboard under Settings → Developer). The secret is used on your
server to sign logged-in visitors’ IDs; it is never put in your pages. No visitor
data is sent with these requests.

10. Disconnecting (DELETE https://relaybell.com/api/v1/keys/current)

When an administrator clicks Disconnect, your server asks relaybell to cancel
the API key that one-click Connect created for this site, so a copy left in a
backup can’t be used. Only the key itself is sent (as the request’s
authorization). A key you entered by hand is left alone.

No data is sent anywhere until you connect (or save a Project ID and API key
manually).
